I'm trying to fit the probelevel model for RMA processed Exon Array
data, and would like to omit the probe affinities term from the model.

If I was using the fitPLM command directly I would be able to specify
something like

Is there a way of specifying this using the aroma.affymetrix framework?
The only argument I can see that vaguely corresponds to this would be
"probeModel" in the ProbeLevelModel class, but this obviously isn't able
to accept models of this form.

The only other way that I can think of would be to fit the model for
each array separately, which would then omit this term from the model by
default.

Do any of the more seasoned hands have any other suggestions?

Thanks in advance,

Steve

Comments below.

>
> Is there a way of specifying this using the aroma.affymetrix framework?
> The only argument I can see that vaguely corresponds to this would be
> "probeModel" in the ProbeLevelModel class, but this obviously isn't able
> to accept models of this form.

In aroma.affymetrix, the PLM that is fit using RmaPlm/ExonRmaPlm is always
the default model (i.e. ~-1 + probes + samples).  All of the standard use
cases (RMA summarization, FIRMA) are covered by this model.

I'm not sure what it is you are trying to do.  Are you taking the
probeset-summarized data (i.e. approximately exon-level) and trying to get
gene-level summaries?  If so, why not use 'mergeGroups=TRUE' with an
appropriately formatted CDF file?

> The only other way that I can think of would be to fit the model for
> each array separately, which would then omit this term from the model by
> default.

Wouldn't this be equivalent to just taking the (robust?) means of each
sample?

> Do any of the more seasoned hands have any other suggestions?

Of course, you can do general linear modeling with lm() and its robust
version rlm() (in the MASS package).

Hope that helps.

Cheers,
Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

Thanks for the response. I'm looking at an experiment with a series of
paired samples, e.g. T cell populations before & after stimulation for a
series of different donors.

The initial analysis I did at the transcript level used the approach of
calculating the logFC between the two samples for each donor then using
these values as the limma input. I guess it's almost the old two-colour
array type approach.

After looking at some plots in Genome Graphs & observing some similar
probe behaviours between the two samples, it just got me to thinking
that I could actually subtract one log-intensity value from the other at
the probe-level for each paired sample, rather than at the transcript
level. If I did this, the PLM would effectively be fitting the logFC as
the value at the transcript level. Algebraically the fitted values for
the probes cancel out & the most appropriate model is then to omit this
term during the PLM fitting, i.e.

For given gene in paired samples 1 & 2, for probes k = 1,...K:

y1k = c1 + pk + e1k
y2k = c2 + pk + e2k

then
xk = y1k - y2k = c1-c2 + e1k-e2k

(Apologies for the crude subscripts. 'c' is the chip effect, 'p' is the
probe effect, 'e' is the error)

I'm really just having a look at this approach, but would like to be
able to do it & then compare it to the conventional FIRMA approach. A
crude pass at it using the default PLM at the transcript level did show
some interesting behaviour (i.e. increased stability of the logFC
estimates between donors). As there is slightly less fitting done under
this method, there may some artefacts that can be avoided as compared to
the usual FIRMA methods.

Hope that didn't sound too crazy, and from what you're saying it doesn't
sound possible at the moment. I was assuming that aroma.affymetrix makes
a call to fitPLM at some point & wondered if there was a way I could
then pass that model on at that point. That may not have been an
accurate assumption though so I'll keep playing & see if I can find a
way to work around it.

 > Wouldn't this be equivalent to just taking the (robust?) means of each
 > sample?

I'm not really sure, I assume that the IRLS calculations during the
fitting would still downweight 'outlier' probes so I guess it would be a
form of taking the robust mean. I'm a bit hazy on the IRLS algorithm though.

My supervisor once said that a PhD is really a license to call yourself
a beginner. In that case I'm still a couple of years away from the
starting line...

Cheers,

Steve

messages.body_plain:
A quick comment:

yes, the fitPLM() of affyPLM is rather flexible, but we don't have a
transparent way for supporting all its features.  It is not too hard
to provide your own aroma.affymetrix wrapper though; people have done
it.  However, if you omit the probe affinities you will end fitting:

   log2(y_ik) = log2(theta_i) + eps_ik

A non-robust estimate is then

  log2(theta_i)* = mean_k(log2(y_ik))

A robust estimate is:

  log2(theta_i)* = median_k(log2(y_ik))

which is equivalent to:

  theta_i* = median_k(y_ik)

and this estimator is provided by:

plm <- AvgPlm(cs);

Note that it, just like RmaPlm(), will fit the model for each unit
group separately.  There is currently no implementation for doing
"mergeGroups=TRUE" of this one.

Does this help

answer all questions soon; the code development is still going forward

messages.body_plain:
Hi Group,

I have been working with some expression arrays. We first did the
analysis in aroma.affymetrix, using RmaBackgroundCorrection,
quantileNormalization and RmaPlm. The arrays come from different
batches. This effect can be seen in the summarized expression.

After the RmaBackgroundCorrection the plotDensity shows that there are
different group and the offset has not been completely removed.
plotDensity(csExprBC, type = “pm”)

We tried to use the function “backgroundCorrect” from the Limma
package using a maximum likelihood estimator for the parameters of the
normexp model. This is what we did:

Ø       aux <- getUnitIntensities(csExpr, stratifyBy="pm");
Ø       aux <- unlist(aux);
Ø       dim(aux) <- c(41, length(aux)/41); # i have 41 samples
Ø       ExprPM <- t(aux) ;

aux will be a matrix with whose size is genes (we used the ensembl cdf
for hgu133plus2) by samples, with only “pm” probes. Once I have the
variable “aux” I call the function from limma:

Ø       ExprBCmle <- backgroundCorrect(ExprPM, method="normexp",
normexp.method="mle",verbose=TRUE);

The density plot result is impressive:

plotDensity(log2(ExprBCmle+50))

All the arrays seem to have almost identical densityplot (without
performing any quantile normalization). We summed up 50 as suggested
in (Gordon Smyth et al., Biostatistics January 2009. Microarray
background correction: maximum likelihood estimation for the normal-
exponential convolution).

So my question is if there is anyway to do this from aroma.affymetrix,
I mean if this backgroundCorrection function is implemented in
aroma.affymetrix? If it is not, can we create a cel file with the
results of this background correction and continue afterwards?
This is the code we used:

# Background removal

> 4.fit(firma)

The short answer is that FIRMA scores are really a probeset-level
statistic, not a gene/transcript-level statistic.  This is the
recommended use of FIRMA.

>  Or with the FIRMA score of each probeset, find out which
> transcripts are differentially expressed.

This statement puzzles me.  FIRMA is really going after differential
*splicing*, not differential expression.  If you want differential
expression, you could do something like:

ces <- getChipEffectSet(plmTr)
gExprs <- extractDataFrame(ces, addNames=TRUE)

... then you can use log2 of the chip effects here for an analysis of
differential expression with an appropriate design matrix with limma.
Is that what you are after?

Alternatively, I am working on a gene-level score for splicing, just
accepted for publication.  This is meant to be applied to the Affy
Gene 1.0 ST arrays (or similar) but could be applied to the Exon
arrays.  This would give a gene-level scoring of splicing.

Cheers,
Mark

Despite GLAD being a good segmentation algorithm, you may want to
consider alternatives that are less computationally intensive and give
equivalent results. CBS (package DNAcopy in bioconductor) runs in 1.5h
for a SNP6.0 array. A fairly new but very promising program is
Ultrasome (http://www.broad.mit.edu/ultrasome). It segments a SNP6.0
array in 2 seconds (plus 1 minute to read the array). It's a
standalone program.

> My problem is the interpretation of the results.
> Here are some examples:
>
> 1. example:
> "chromosome"  "start"       "stop"        "mean"        "count"       "call"

> 1         10546623        10546623       -2.21390332082091       1      "loss"
> 1         10548849        21751915       0.150400582947561       6872   "neutral"
>
> This example has two regions where start=stop position (10544961,
> 10546623).
> How do you interpret this result?
> How should regions with count=1 be interpreted?
> Are these two regions considered to be outliers?

SNP6.0 arrays are very noisy. You should be very careful when you
consider any segment that has a size < 10 probes, and in any case, you
should not believe any segment that has a size of one probe. In your

as "outliers" by GLAD.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sabrina.

Sorry for the delay in response.

On 13/04/2009, at 5:40 AM, sabrina wrote:

> Hi, all:
> I am trying to understand the supplementary text of the original FIRMA
> paper published in Bioinformatics last year. the S1 figure shows UNR
> gene about its exon effect removed or retained. I am confused about
> the plots. what are the y-axis? Are they  residuals from RMA fit ,
> after running ExonRMAPlm?

No, they are not residuals.  For one, residuals will be positive and
negative.  What you see in Figure S1 are all positive.  To use your
symbols below, the model can be written:

d = c + p + r

d - log2 intensity
c - chip effect
p - probe effect
r - residual

Sometimes we plot residuals:

r = d - c - p

Sometimes we plot the data on the original scale, after removing probe
effects (like Figure S1a):

d - p  (i.e. leaving the chip effect in)

Figure S1b is plotting is a slight modification to this.  What it says
in the text (and Elizabeth can correct me here if I've got it wrong)
is that the probe effects also absorb any exon effect.  And so, p can
actually be broken down into e + p* (where e is an exon effect and p*
is a probe effect that is nested within the exon).  Figure S1b is
plotting:

d - p*

or, equivalently:

d - p + e

And for those plots, the exon effect e is estimated as the median of
the original probe effects p, for a given exon.

Does that make sense?

> Let d be the normalized intensity (log2), r as the residual from plm
> fit (log2), p as the probe affinity.   I would assume S1(a) is just
> simple plot of d-p, S1(b) as d-p+estimated e(j)? Am I correct? If that
> is the case, S1(a) should show exact same information as plot of d
> because for all arrays, the probe affinity should be the same?

True, the probe effects are estimated for each probe and are the same
for every sample.  However, S1a (a plot of *d-p*) will not look the
same as a plot of *d*, since for each probe (x-value in the plot), a
different number is subtracted.

> But
> from the figures, how can I tell where the splicing events occur? I am
> puzzled because I thought it should also remove gene effect (chip
> effect)? Can some one explain it to me?

Keep in mind that the manuscript says, right after this point about
exon effects, that "The FIRMA scores could be adjusted to include this
information [exon effects] but so far we are not convinced that the
data is clean enough for the benefits to outweigh the additional
noise." ... and indeed, the FIRMA scores do remove the gene effect,
since the FIRMA score is a summary of the residuals for each
probeset.  The plots sometimes keep the chip effects in because it is
illustrative.

Hope that helps.
Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mathieu.

One of the things that I highly recommend you do for quality assessment of
Affy exon/expression arrays is the RLE and NUSE plots.

Look for the "Quality assessment of PLM fit" section of:
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/human-exon-array-analysis

Briefly, if you've fit the PLM models already, you can plot these
directly:

[...]

plmTr <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
fit(plmTr, verbose=verbose)

qamTr <- QualityAssessmentModel(plmTr)
plotNuse(qamTr)
plotRle(qamTr)

Alternatively, you can always look at boxplots or densities of various
things.  Below is one example:

plotDensity(cs)
plotDensity(csN)

# extract raw intensities from AffymetrixCelSet
d <- extractMatrix(cs,verbose=verbose)
boxplot( as.data.frame( log2(d) ) )

# extract normalized intensities from AffymetrixCelSet
dN <- extractMatrix(csN,verbose=verbose)
boxplot( as.data.frame( log2(dN) ) )

... and so on.

Note that you may want to limit yourself to densities/boxplots of only
probes that are part of 'core' probesets, as opposed to 'full', 'extended'
or controls.  You can do this with the 'subset' argument of plotDensity()
and the 'cells' argument of extractMatrix().

Hope that gets you started.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jing,
I would actually recommmend using the smaller cdf *if* there is no
downstream need for the remaining probes to be normalized. Generally it
doesn't seem to matter, but probes at background are not always
sensitive to certain types of differences between arrays compared to
those with signal and thus you can wind up with normalized data that
looks very different when you look at just the smaller set of probes
(and even with just core probes, you always have enough low-expressing
genes to be representative of background signal as well). Ideally you
could use this normalization on a smaller set and back normalize for the
other probes, but I don't think this is implemented in aroma.affymetrix.
Best,
Elizabeth

messages.body_plain:
Hi Anbarasu.

You can find out more about extractMatrix() and readUnits() via the
following:

?extractMatrix.AffymetrixCelSet

?readUnits.AffymetrixCelFile

For quality assessment, you might also look at RLE and NUSE plots from
the PLM fits.

For extractMatrix(), maybe you only want to pull out intensities just
the core probes.  If you call extractMatrix() with 'cells=NULL' (the
default), you are trying to read ALL probes and all samples into
memory.  Back of the envelope calculation (6M probes, 150 samples, 8
byte float):

 > 6000000*150*8/1024^2
[1] 6866.455

is nearly 7GB, plus a little bit of overhead.  So, it's no surprise
that that won't fly on your 4G machine.  However, maybe you just want
the ~1M core probes (or even a random sampling).  One way to do this
with extractMatrix() is:

cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType(chipType,
tag="coreR3,A20071112,EP")

# get the indices of just the core probesets
cellIndices <- getCellIndices(cdf, unlist=TRUE, useNames=FALSE)

# extract data for only these probes  (about 8MB of memory per sample)
d <- extractMatrix(cs, cells=cellIndices,verbose=-50)

... could do boxplots of intensity:

boxplot( as.data.frame(log2(d)) )

.... or maybe 100K probes is enough to get a feel for what the samples
are doing ...

s <- sample(cellIndices, 100000)

# extract data for only these probes  (about 750KB of memory per sample)
d <- extractMatrix(cs, cells=s,verbose=-50)

.... and replace 'cs' above here with 'csBC', 'csN', or whatever
AffymetrixCelSet object you are interested in.

Just some thoughts.

Hope that helps.
Mark

aberration.  In this case, maybe you just want to look for large-in-
magnitude FIRMA scores.

... maybe you also want to look at interesting probesets via
GenomeGraphs:

Mark

Hi,

Following on from my question a few weeks back.

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/browse_thread/thread/6697da560b150509#

effects have been omitted from the model, by using rlm (MASS) with the
same settings as fitPLM (affyPLM). I've also set it up so the data
output has the same structure as if I'd used ExonRmaPlm with
mergeGroups=TRUE, i.e. I have used a CEL file based on the monocell cdf
to store the Chip Effects, and I've also generated a blank CEL file
called "probeAffinities.CEL". The folder structure is also identical.

The calculations for the residuals & FIRMA scores should now be the same
as if the default model had fitted, so I'm wondering if there is a way I
can coerce what I have (i.e. a collection of CEL files containing the
key data) into an object such as an ExonRmaPlm Model so that I can then
apply methods such as getResidualSet() and FirmaModel().

Thanks in advance,

Steve

Hi Sabrina.

I have not had to deal with this myself, but I do know that it exists
and I can at least suggest a possible route to exclude affected exons.

Presumably, there is a database (dbSNP?) that tells you the genome
locations of each SNP for your strains.  There is also a probe.tab
file from Affymetrix that gives you the mapped genome locations of
each probe (or you could take the sequences from the same file and map
them yourself with a tool like BLAT).  It is then just a matter of
looking whether each probe maps to a location on the genome that
overlaps a SNP.  There is probably a Bioconductor tool for this or you
could create a hash, etc.

There are a couple levels at which you might introduce this to your
analysis.  You could remove individual probes that are affected.  On
the aroma.affymetrix side, this would require creating a new CDF with
those affected probes not included (a bit tricky but doable).  Or, you
could simply post-process your existing results and remove probesets
that have an affected probe (easier but not as elegant).

You might've also seen:

Duan S, Zhang W, Bleibel WK, Cox NJ, Dolan ME: SNPinProbe 1.0: A
database for filtering out
probes in the Affymetrix GeneChip(R) Human Exon 1.0 ST array
potentially affected by SNPs.
Bioinformation 2008, 2(10):469{470.

Hope that gets you started.

Cheers,
Mark
